labels.why: Agents change tickets through the HTTP API, so merge needs a method, route, ticket identifiers, success response and the API's usual unknown-field check.
The choice of survivor determines which ticket agents continue working on, so callers need to know how that choice is made.
Whether the agent's judgment suffices determines which pairs the merge accepts, including tickets with different titles or requesters.
The absorbed ticket needs a defined state so the existing edit and transition operations can handle later requests consistently.
A merge of tickets with different field values needs a rule for what the survivor retains and where the absorbed requester's identity remains visible.
Clients can still request the absorbed ID or list tickets by status, so both read paths need defined results and a way to identify the survivor.
Eligibility depends on both tickets' states and whether their IDs coincide, and each refusal must fit the API's invalid-request or state-conflict rules.
Either ticket reference can fail validation or lookup, and the error envelope must let the caller identify which input needs correction.
Later merges can involve either member of an earlier pair, so the rules must keep survivor links resolvable and prevent cycles.
A caller can retry after losing the first response, so the second result and its effects on the audit log are part of the merge contract.
The store ties timestamps and audit entries to actual changes, so the specification must say what counts as a change to the survivor.
The request names agents, so the access rule must identify what the internal network enforces and what the caller-supplied X-Actor header contributes to attribution.
Persistence explicitly selects ticket fields on save and load, so the link needs a durable representation and a defined reading for older version 1 records.
The loader validates saved records at startup, so it needs rules for dangling targets, cycles and inconsistent states, with errors identifying the offending record.
The audit endpoint retrieves entries by ticket ID, so the merge must define what each history shows about the actor, action and field changes.
A partial merge could leave ticket state out of sync with its history or outbox, so all effects must commit together in memory and in the configured data file.
The existing outbox can hold pending events for the absorbed ticket, and any merge notice uses that same system's recipients, templates and deduplication keys.
Operators already use show and list to inspect saved tickets, so how those commands display an absorbed ticket and its destination is part of the change.
Operators need to know whether a mistaken merge is final and what correction is possible while preserving audit history and ticket numbers.
Merge shares the store, lifecycle, listing and audit code with ordinary ticket operations, whose existing contracts must continue to hold.
The weekly report reads status and priority by column position and counts each raw line, so column order and the inclusion of absorbed tickets affect its totals.

Merge changes the documented API and store semantics, bringing success, error and atomicity tests, API documentation, a decision record and release updates within the project's dependency-free TicketStore conventions.
